Lecture slides and notes, organized by the parts of the [course schedule](mlesyllabus26.qmd#course-schedule). New decks are added as the semester proceeds.

## Part I — Foundations

- **Before Week 1.** [Linear Model Prediction Methods](predictionOLS26.qmd) — prediction and quantities of interest in the linear model (at-means and average effects; ML, delta, and simulation-based uncertainty), previewing the methods we generalize to nonlinear models.
- **Week 1.** [Binary Response Models](binarymodels26.qmd) — building a maximum-likelihood model for a binary outcome: why the linear probability model fails, the latent-variable and random-utility motivations, the likelihood and link functions, and interpretation via predicted probabilities, marginal effects, and odds.
- **Week 2.** [Likelihood Theory & Estimation Mechanics](likelihood26.qmd) — what a likelihood is and how it differs from a probability; the estimation machine and how little of it changes from one model to the next; analytic methods and closed-form solutions, and where they fail; and the two derivatives — the score and the Hessian — that locate the estimate and set its standard error.
- **Week 3.** [Maximizing the Log-Likelihood Function](llfmax26.qmd) — Newton–Raphson from the ground up: where the method comes from, what its two halves do, one step worked by hand, then the whole loop run to convergence on a real logit, with an animated climb, the iteration log, starting values, and the properties that justify the estimator.

## Part II — Binomial extensions, and a causal lens

- **Week 4.** [Prediction Methods for MLE Models](prediction26.qmd) — quantities of interest from nonlinear models: at-means and average effects, building a scenario's linear prediction, King–Tomz–Wittenberg simulation, ML and delta-method standard errors with end-point transformation, the bootstrap, average effects bounded two ways, and guidance on which approach and which technique to choose.
- **Week 4.** [Diagnostics, Classification, and Fit](binaryextensions126.qmd) — what to check after a binary-response model is fitted: whether the link's symmetry assumption suits the data, how classification and ROC curves work and why they mean more for a House roll call than for democratic peace models, how separation breaks the estimator (especially when you add fixed effects), rare-events bias and the Firth correction, and the trinity of tests with the information criteria.
- **Week 5.** [Discrete-Time Hazards](discretehazards26.qmd) — relaxing temporal independence in binary models: what memory would look like, the hazard rate and the concepts under it (failure, survival, censoring, spells), BTSCS data and the Beck–Katz–Tucker fix, three baseline hazards from constant to cubic, the same machinery on leader tenure, how to present hazard results as survivor functions and median survival times, competing risks when the event has kinds, and transition models as a different kind of memory.
- **Week 6.** [Interactions in Nonlinear Models](interactions26.qmd) — why nonlinear models are interactive in all of their variables whether or not you say so: compression as a property of the link, what a multiplicative term adds that compression cannot, predicted probabilities and marginal effects and the difference between a derivative and a discrete change, and the two questions a conditional-effect plot cannot answer on its own — whether the functional form is right, and whether the cases it describes exist.
- **Week 7.** [A Causal Lens on the Binomial](causallens26.qmd) — reading the logit and its quantities of interest causally: potential outcomes and estimands, why a raw difference mixes the effect with selection bias, DAGs as a way to decide what to condition on (confounders, mediators, colliders), two ways to remove selection bias (g-computation, which is the average marginal effect, and propensity-score weighting) and the doubly-robust estimator that combines them, and where selection on observables sits beside the design-based methods.
- **Week 7.** [A Second Causal Example: Parental Divorce and Infidelity](causalinfidelity26.qmd) — the same selection-on-observables steps on non-political data from the General Social Survey: does growing up with divorced parents raise the chance of straying in one's own marriage? A DAG with a cohort confounder that pushes the bias the other way, post-treatment traps that look like background controls, all three estimators and how to choose among them, and a selection model for a sample that only includes the married.

## Part III — Counts and durations as one family

- **Week 8.** [Count Models I](countA26.qmd) — modeling a count of events: where the Poisson comes from as the limit of the binomial and what that derivation assumes, the Poisson regression and its quantities of interest (rate ratios, expected counts, probabilities of particular counts) on violent social conflict in Africa, exposure and the offset, equidispersion and how to check it, the negative binomial and what its dispersion parameter is telling you about the specification, and how the same events can be counted, timed, or recorded period by period — and why those three data structures lead to models that are related in exact ways.
- **Week 8, extended example.** [Traffic Cameras in DC](dccameras26.qmd) — the count models on a policy question: do DC's traffic cameras fall more heavily on Black neighborhoods? Where the cameras go (cameras per census tract, nearly Poisson) and how many tickets each writes (tickets per camera, badly overdispersed), with the likelihoods written out, a negative binomial estimated by hand, exposure as an estimated coefficient versus an offset, interactive maps, and a hurdle model that puts the two stages together.
- **Week 9.** [Count Models II](countB26.qmd) — when the zeros come from two processes: opportunity and willingness on every pair of states, 1951–1985, the negative binomial as a continuous mixture and the zero-inflated and hurdle models as discrete ones, structural and sampling zeros, the zero-inflated Poisson and negative binomial, the hurdle model and the Poisson as a hurdle with its two parts tied together, choosing between them, quantities of interest from two equations at once, estimating which dyads have the opportunity to fight, and a zero-inflated model of US uses of force revisited twenty years on.
